summary: Plans a multi-year phaseout of the 6bone, the IPv6 testbed network that the IETF established in 1996, along with its 3FFE::/16 address allocation. IPv6 was starting production deployment, so testing space could be retired. It obsoletes RFC 2471 and is informational.

eli5.summary: The 6bone was a practice track for IPv6 before the real roads were built. This is the schedule for taking the practice track down once the real roads are open.

subtitle: Plan to shut down the IPv6 testbed network and reclaim its address space.

tldr.problem: The 6bone, an IPv6 testbed network established in 1996, needs to be phased out as production IPv6 deployment is now underway.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC establishes a multi-year phaseout schedule: new address allocations stop in January 2004, all 6bone addresses are reclaimed by June 2006.
tldr.outcome: The 6bone was successfully retired on schedule, and its 3FFE::/16 address block was reclaimed for reuse. The network served its purpose in helping IPv6 transition.

today: The 6bone was successfully phased out and all 3FFE::/16 prefixes were reclaimed on schedule. It served its purpose in enabling IPv6 protocol testing and deployment planning during the transition from IPv4.

sections.title: The 6bone Testbed
sections.content:
The 6bone was an experimental network established in March 1996 to test IPv6 protocols before they were deployed on the production Internet. It operated as a separate testbed using a dedicated address allocation: initially 5F00::/8, then 3FFE::/16 starting in 1998.

The 6bone served multiple purposes: it allowed protocol developers and implementers to test their IPv6 code, enabled experimentation with IPv6 routing practices, allowed organizations to test IPv6 applications, and provided early users a safe place to try IPv6 networking. By the time RFC 3701 was written in 2004, production IPv6 deployment was underway, making the testbed less critical.
sections.eli5: The 6bone was like a practice track where engineers could test new IPv6 roads before anyone used them for real traffic.

sections.title: Addressing History
sections.content:
The 6bone started in 1996 with the address block 5F00::/8 under the original provider-based unicast address format. In 1998, the IPv6 Addressing Architecture was revised, and the 6bone was re-addressed to use the new Aggregatable Global Unicast Address format under 3FFE::/16. This re-addressing happened smoothly in the fall of 1998.

From 1998 onwards, the 6bone operated using the 3FFE::/16 prefix with a hierarchical allocation system. The RFC explicitly acknowledged that these addresses were temporary and would be reclaimed when the testbed was no longer needed.
sections.eli5: The practice track had two versions of road signs. In 1998, they changed to a new style, but kept the same practice track running.

sections.title: Why Phaseout Now
sections.content:
By 2002, production IPv6 address prefixes allocated by Regional Internet Registries (RIRs) had surpassed the total 6bone allocations. This indicated sufficient interest in production IPv6 that the testbed was no longer the primary driver of IPv6 development.

However, the RFC acknowledges that some continuing need existed for the 6bone, as various testbed users still depended on it. The phaseout plan therefore allocates several years to allow users to transition from 6bone addresses to production IPv6 prefixes allocated by their regional registries.
sections.eli5: By 2002, the real IPv6 roads had enough addresses handed out that the practice track was no longer the main event. But some people still needed time to move from the practice track to the real roads.

sections.title: The Phaseout Schedule
sections.content:
The plan established two key dates:

January 1, 2004: No new 6bone address allocations (pTLAs, or pseudo Top-Level Aggregators) are permitted. Existing allocations may continue to be used but no new ones are assigned.

June 6, 2006: All 6bone prefixes from the 3FFE::/16 space are reclaimed and cease operation. After this date, network operators are encouraged to filter traffic using 3FFE:: prefixes to ensure they are not misused.

The RFC allows three years between the allocation cutoff and the operational cutoff, giving 6bone users sufficient time to transition their networks to production IPv6 addresses.
sections.eli5: Starting January 2004, nobody can get a new pass to the practice track. Everyone has until June 2006 to move their infrastructure to the real roads.

sections.title: Implementation and Transition
sections.content:
The RFC does not specify any particular transition mechanism or requirements for prefix renumbering. Organizations are free to seek production IPv6 addresses at any hierarchical level that matches their needs, whether that is a larger prefix or a smaller one.

The RFC notes lessons from IPv4 history: when IPv4 addresses are reclaimed and potentially reallocated, network operators may be reluctant to remove filters, even long after the addresses are no longer in use. IANA is advised to consider this when deciding whether to reallocate the 3FFE::/16 block in the future.
sections.eli5: Organizations can choose what size of production address block works best for them. And when the old practice block gets freed up, people might block it forever by accident, so maybe it is better to just not use it again.
